reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Middleton's Allergy
clinicalPearls: Selective IgA deficiency is the most common primary immunodeficiency and is defined by a very low or absent serum IgA with normal IgG and IgM and otherwise intact immunity
The majority of affected individuals are asymptomatic and are detected incidentally, so a low IgA alone does not equate to clinical disease
When symptomatic, patients tend to have recurrent sinopulmonary and gastrointestinal infections, reflecting the loss of secretory IgA at mucosal surfaces
There is a recognised association with atopy and with autoimmune conditions such as coeliac disease, so unexplained IgA deficiency warrants screening for these
Coeliac serology based on IgA antibodies can be falsely negative in IgA deficiency, so IgG-based testing or histology should be used instead
A minority have severe anaphylactic reactions to blood products because of anti-IgA antibodies, so washed or IgA-deficient blood components may be required
There is no specific replacement therapy because IgA cannot be effectively replaced; management centres on prompt treatment of infections and, where needed, prophylactic antibiotics
A small proportion, particularly those with associated IgG subclass deficiency or poor vaccine responses, can progress over time toward common variable immunodeficiency and need monitoring
reference.pathophysiology: Selective IgA deficiency results from a failure of terminal differentiation of IgA-committed B cells into IgA-secreting plasma cells, so that little or no IgA reaches serum and mucosal secretions. The loss of secretory IgA impairs mucosal immune exclusion of pathogens at the respiratory and gastrointestinal surfaces, though compensatory secretory IgM often limits the clinical impact. The precise molecular basis is usually unknown; it shares genetic susceptibility loci (including MHC haplotypes and TACI variants) with CVID, and the two conditions can occur within the same families and occasionally evolve into one another. Immune dysregulation underlies the associated atopic and autoimmune disease.
additionalDifferentials: Common variable immunodeficiency (may share features and can evolve from IgA deficiency)
Transient low IgA in early childhood before immune maturation
IgG subclass or specific antibody deficiency presenting with recurrent infection
Coeliac disease and other associated autoimmune disorders
additionalInvestigations: Serum IgA, IgG, and IgM to confirm isolated IgA deficiency
IgG subclass levels and vaccine-specific antibody responses to assess for broader deficiency
Coeliac evaluation using IgG-based serology or duodenal biopsy given unreliable IgA-based tests
Screening for associated autoimmune disease when clinically indicated
Testing for anti-IgA antibodies before transfusion in patients with prior reactions
Periodic reassessment of immunoglobulins to detect evolution toward CVID
redFlags: Anaphylactic transfusion reaction from anti-IgA antibodies, requiring IgA-deficient or washed blood products
Progressive fall in IgG or poor vaccine responses signalling evolution to CVID
Recurrent severe or invasive infection prompting reassessment of the full antibody profile
Unexplained malabsorption or systemic autoimmune features suggesting an associated disorder
reference.prognosis: Most individuals with selective IgA deficiency remain well and have a normal life expectancy. Symptomatic patients generally do well with treatment of infections, but a subset with additional immune defects have more infections and may progress to CVID, and rare transfusion anaphylaxis is a serious hazard.
pitfalls: Interpreting an incidental low IgA as clinically significant disease in an asymptomatic person
Missing coeliac disease because of falsely negative IgA-based serology
Transfusing standard blood products in a patient with anti-IgA antibodies
Failing to reassess immunoglobulins over time and thus missing progression to CVID
management: Treat recurrent sinopulmonary and gastrointestinal infections promptly with appropriate antibiotics, as immunoglobulin replacement is not indicated for isolated deficiency
Consider prophylactic antibiotics for frequent or severe recurrent infections
Screen for and manage associated coeliac disease using IgG-based serology or duodenal biopsy, and other autoimmune conditions
Transfuse washed or IgA-deficient blood components in patients with anti-IgA antibodies or prior transfusion reactions
Reserve immunoglobulin replacement for those who evolve to CVID or have a proven additional antibody defect
Monitor immunoglobulins periodically to detect progression toward CVID
Provide patient education and a medical alert regarding transfusion reaction risk
